guidance: Use it when a manifest, a kubectl description or an incident note gives CPU or memory in units you want as plain numbers. CPU counts cores, memory counts bytes, and case matters: M is a million bytes while m is a thousandth, so 400m of memory is 0.4 bytes and almost always means 400Mi. The total adds the lines exactly as Kubernetes stores them, after rounding any value finer than 0.001, and the page says when it does.
method: Every line is read with the Quantity grammar documented by the Kubernetes API reference: an optional plus or minus sign, a decimal number that may be written 12, 12.5 or .5, an optional decimal exponent such as 1e3, and an optional suffix, which the grammar makes an alternative to the exponent. The suffixes are m for one thousandth, k, M, G, T, P and E for 10^3 through 10^18, and Ki, Mi, Gi, Ti, Pi and Ei for 2^10 through 2^60. Parsing splits the digits into a BigInt mantissa and a decimal scale and multiplies in the suffix factor, so 250m becomes 250 with scale 3, 1.5Gi becomes 1610612736, and 129e6 becomes 129000000 without any floating-point step. The value is normalised by removing trailing zeros, and the magnitude is checked against 2^63-1, the limit the reference states for a single Quantity; anything larger is refused rather than capped silently. Kubernetes keeps at most three decimal places and rounds more precise values up in magnitude, so a parsed value with a larger scale is rounded up to the nearest 0.001 before it is displayed or summed, which is the documented 0.1m becoming 1m, and the page prints a warning naming the original value. The lines are then added by aligning their scales, so the total is the arithmetic sum of the stored lines: no per-line figure is rounded again and no fraction is dropped. For CPU the total is reported in cores and in millicores, the unit of 0.001 core that Kubernetes requires for fractions; binary and power-of-ten suffixes are refused for CPU because CPU is counted in cores, matching the documentation. For memory and storage the total is reported in bytes together with the largest exact binary multiple and, when the total is not an exact multiple, a two-decimal approximation marked with a tilde; memory quantities below one byte are flagged, and a bare m suffix on memory is called out as the 0.4-byte mistake the documentation warns about. Lines may carry a name before an equals sign for readability, a leading hash marks a comment, at most 40 quantities and 4,000 characters are accepted, and the page does no network access.

sources.title: Kubernetes API reference: Quantity — the serialization grammar (Ki to Ei, m and k to E, or a decimal exponent), the 2^63-1 magnitude limit, and the rule that values with more than three decimal places round up, so 0.1m becomes 1m.

Kubernetes documentation: Resource Management for Pods and Containers — CPU is measured in cores, where 0.1 equals 100m and precision finer than 1m is not allowed; memory is measured in bytes with the suffixes E, P, T, G, M, k or Ei, Pi, Ti, Gi, Mi, Ki, and 400m of memory means 0.4 bytes.

kubernetes/apimachinery: pkg/api/resource/quantity.go — the Quantity implementation that parses these strings, keeps three decimal places of precision, and canonicalises 1.5 as 1500m and 1.5Gi as 1536Mi.
